Judges 1.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew the tribes still lived beside Canaanite peoples. This chapter explained why that unfinished conquest mattered to their life in the land.

culture.title: Cutting off thumbs and toes
culture.text: Cutting off a captive's thumbs and big toes made him unable to fight or run. Adonibezek says he had done the same to seventy kings.

culture.title: Forced labor
culture.text: Defeated peoples were often made to work as forced laborers ("tributaries"). Solomon later used Canaanites this way (1 Kings 9:20–21).

Judges 2.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew the recurring trouble of serving other gods. This chapter explained the pattern of rebellion, oppression, rescue, and relapse behind those troubles.

culture.title: Baal and Ashtaroth
culture.text: Baal was the Canaanite storm god believed to bring rain and fertility. Ashtaroth (Ashtoreth) was a goddess of fertility and war. Farmers who depended on rain were drawn to their worship.

culture.title: Judges
culture.text: The "judges" were deliverers and leaders raised up in times of crisis, not mainly courtroom officials. Most led one region or a few tribes.

Judges 3.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Israel had faced stronger neighbors. They heard how the LORD raised deliverers from Judah, Benjamin, and elsewhere when Israel cried out.

culture.title: Left-handed warriors
culture.text: Ehud was left-handed, so he wore his dagger on his right thigh, where guards would not expect it. Benjamin was known for left-handed fighters (Judges 20:16).

culture.title: Bringing tribute
culture.text: Subject peoples brought tribute—goods and silver—to their overlord. Ehud uses the occasion to gain a private audience with Eglon.

culture.title: An ox goad
culture.text: An ox goad was a long pole with a metal point used to drive oxen. Shamgar used one as a weapon.

Judges 4.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Hazor and the northern plain. They heard that the LORD defeated a chariot army through Deborah, Barak, and Jael.

culture.title: Iron chariots
culture.text: Sisera had nine hundred chariots fitted with iron. Chariots were the most powerful weapons on the flat plains, such as the Jezreel valley, where this battle took place.

culture.title: Tent pegs and hospitality
culture.text: Women in herding families usually pitched the tents, so Jael would be skilled with a tent pin and hammer. A guest normally expected protection in a host's tent.

culture.title: The Kenites
culture.text: The Kenites were a nomadic people related to Moses' father-in-law Hobab. Heber had moved away from the rest of the Kenites.

Judges 5.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew which tribes answered the call to fight and which did not. The song taught them to remember the LORD's victory and the cost of refusing to help.

culture.title: Victory songs
culture.text: Victory songs celebrated battles and spread the news of them. Women often composed and led them, as Miriam did (Exodus 15:20–21).

culture.title: The Kishon in flood
culture.text: The river Kishon runs through the Jezreel valley. Heavy rain could turn the plain to mud and make chariots useless.

Judges 6.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew the fear of raids and lost harvests. They heard why Israel's disobedience mattered and how the LORD called Gideon while he was afraid.

culture.title: Threshing in a winepress
culture.text: Grain was normally threshed on an open hilltop where the wind could carry away the chaff. Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress, a sunken pit, to hide it from the Midianites.

culture.title: Camel raiders
culture.text: Camels let raiders cross the desert quickly and in large numbers. This is one of the earliest descriptions of camels used in warfare.

culture.title: A fleece on the threshing floor
culture.text: Wool absorbs dew overnight. Gideon asks for dew on the fleece only, then on the ground only.

Judges 7.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew that a small force could not defeat a great camp by strength alone. They heard that the LORD gave the victory so Israel could not claim it for itself.

culture.title: Trumpets, pitchers, and lamps
culture.text: Each man carried a ram's-horn trumpet and a torch hidden in a clay jar. Smashing the jars and blowing the trumpets at night made 300 men sound like a great army.

culture.title: Night watches
culture.text: The night was divided into watches. Gideon attacks at the beginning of the middle watch, just after the guards were changed.

Judges 8.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Gideon as a deliverer. They also knew the warning that his ephod became a snare, even after he refused the title of king.

culture.title: Crescent ornaments
culture.text: The "ornaments" on the camels' necks were crescent-shaped—moon symbols worn as decorations or charms. Midianite kings wore them too (Judges 8:26).

culture.title: Gold earrings
culture.text: The text notes that the Midianites wore gold earrings "because they were Ishmaelites," a custom of those desert peoples.

Judges 9.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Shechem and the danger of violent rulers. They heard how Abimelech and the people who supported him were repaid for their evil.

culture.title: A fable
culture.text: Jotham's story of trees choosing a king is a fable—a story with plants or animals that teaches a lesson. It is one of the few fables in the Bible.

culture.title: Millstone from a tower
culture.text: A woman drops an upper millstone—the hand-held stone used for grinding grain—from the tower. Being killed by a woman was seen as a disgrace for a warrior (Judges 9:54).

culture.title: Sowing with salt
culture.text: Abimelech sows the destroyed city with salt, a symbolic act of curse known from ancient Near Eastern texts.

Judges 10.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Israel had served the gods of neighboring peoples. They heard that turning from those gods was part of their plea for deliverance.

culture.title: Thirty sons on thirty donkeys
culture.text: Riding donkeys was a sign of status for leaders and their families. Jair's thirty sons each had a donkey and a town.

Judges 11.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Gilead and its conflict with Ammon. They heard both Jephthah's rescue and the grief that followed his careless vow.

culture.title: An outcast son
culture.text: As the son of a prostitute, Jephthah was driven out by his half-brothers so he would not share the inheritance.

culture.title: Vows
culture.text: Vows to a god before battle were common in the ancient world. Israel's law treated vows as binding (Numbers 30:2) but forbade human sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21).

culture.title: Territorial arguments
culture.text: Jephthah speaks of land each people's god had given them. Chemosh was the god of Moab; the Moabite Stone also credits Chemosh with giving land to Moab.

Judges 12.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew the tribes could turn their weapons on one another. They heard how Ephraim's quarrel with Gilead brought terrible loss within Israel.

culture.title: Shibboleth
culture.text: Shibboleth means ‘ear of grain’ or ‘stream.’ Ephraimites pronounced the first sound as "s," so the way they said the word revealed where they were from. "Shibboleth" is still used in English for a test word.

culture.title: Large families
culture.text: Ibzan arranges marriages for thirty sons and thirty daughters with people outside his clan, building alliances through marriage.

Judges 13.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew the Philistines oppressed the border towns of Dan. They heard that Samson was set apart before birth to begin Israel's rescue.

culture.title: A Nazarite from birth
culture.text: Most Nazarite vows were temporary (Numbers 6). Samson is to be a Nazarite from birth, and his mother is to avoid wine and unclean food during pregnancy.

culture.title: Asking a messenger's name
culture.text: Knowing a name meant knowing something about a person's nature. The angel replies that his name is "secret"—the word means wonderful.

Judges 14.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Israel's law warned against marriage with the peoples of the land. They heard how Samson's choice opened a conflict with the Philistines.

culture.title: Wedding feast
culture.text: Wedding celebrations lasted seven days. The groom was attended by companions, and riddles were a popular entertainment at feasts.

culture.title: Changes of garments
culture.text: Fine clothing was valuable property. Samson's wager of thirty sheets (linen garments) and thirty changes of clothing was a large stake.

Judges 15.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew the Philistines ruled over Judah. They heard that the LORD gave Samson strength, even while revenge made the conflict worse.

culture.title: Burning standing grain
culture.text: Destroying an enemy's grain fields, vineyards, and olive groves at harvest was a devastating attack on their food supply.

culture.title: Jawbone
culture.text: A fresh jawbone of a donkey is heavy and hard. Samson names the place Ramath-lehi, ‘hill of the jawbone.’

Judges 16.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Philistine power and the worship of Dagon. They heard that Samson's strength was not his own and that he called on God at the end.

culture.title: City gates
culture.text: City gates were massive wooden doors with bars, set in a stone gateway. Carrying them off was a humiliating act against a city.

culture.title: Grinding in the prison
culture.text: Prisoners were set to grind grain, the work of slaves and women. Blinding captives was practiced in the ancient Near East (2 Kings 25:7).

culture.title: Temple pillars
culture.text: Philistine temples excavated at Tell Qasile had roofs supported by two central wooden pillars on stone bases.

Judges 17.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew the difference between the LORD's worship and private idols. They heard Micah's household as an example of each person doing what seemed right.

culture.title: Household shrines
culture.text: Micah has a house of gods, an ephod, and teraphim, and makes his son a priest. Private shrines were common in the ancient world but contrary to Israel's law.

culture.title: A hired Levite
culture.text: Micah pays a wandering Levite ten shekels a year, clothing, and food to serve as his priest.

Judges 18.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Dan as Israel's northern border. They heard how the tribe's search for land led to stolen worship and violence against Laish.

culture.title: A quiet city
culture.text: Laish was isolated and unguarded, "quiet and secure," with no alliances to call for help.

culture.title: Spies
culture.text: Sending spies to survey land before attacking was standard practice, as Moses and Joshua had done (Numbers 13; Joshua 2).

Judges 19.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Gibeah as a town in Benjamin. They heard this account as proof of how far Israel had fallen when there was no king.

culture.title: Waiting in the town square
culture.text: Travelers without a host waited in the open square of a town hoping to be invited in. No one in Gibeah offered the Levite shelter until an old man from Ephraim did.

culture.title: A concubine
culture.text: A concubine was a wife of lower status, often without a dowry or full inheritance rights for her children.

Judges 20.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew the tribes of Israel and the shame of Gibeah. They heard how Benjamin's refusal to surrender the guilty led to a war that nearly destroyed a tribe.

culture.title: Slingers
culture.text: Benjamin had 700 left-handed slingers who could "sling stones at an hair breadth." Slings were deadly weapons; David later killed Goliath with one.

culture.title: The ark at Bethel
culture.text: The ark was at Bethel at this time, with Phinehas the grandson of Aaron serving as priest—showing these events happened early in the period of the judges.

Judges 21.audience: The first Israelites who heard Judges knew Benjamin survived and remained part of Israel. They heard that rash vows and violent plans did not repair the wrongs of the war.

culture.title: Vineyard festival at Shiloh
culture.text: A yearly feast at Shiloh included young women dancing in the vineyards, probably at the grape harvest.

culture.title: Jabesh-gilead
culture.text: Jabesh-gilead failed to send men and was punished. The town later had close ties to Saul, who rescued it (1 Samuel 11), and its men buried him (1 Samuel 31:11–13).

Ruth 1.audience: The first Israelites who heard Ruth knew Moab lay east of the Dead Sea and that widows without sons were vulnerable. They heard Ruth's choice to join Naomi as a striking act of loyal love.

culture.title: Widows without sons
culture.text: Women depended on husbands and sons for land and protection. A widow with no sons faced poverty.

culture.title: Returning to a mother's house
culture.text: A young widow normally returned to her family to be remarried. Naomi urges her daughters-in-law to go home for that reason.

culture.title: Bethlehem
culture.text: Bethlehem means ‘house of bread,’ a farming town in Judah. The family left during a famine there.

Ruth 2.audience: The first Israelites who heard Ruth knew gleaning laws that provided food for the poor. They heard Boaz use his standing and field to protect a foreign widow.

culture.title: Gleaning
culture.text: The poor followed the reapers, picking up stalks of grain left behind. It was hard work but gave them food.

culture.title: An ephah of barley
culture.text: Ruth gleans about an ephah of barley in one day—roughly two-thirds of a bushel (about 22 liters), a remarkable amount for one gleaner.

culture.title: Greetings in the field
culture.text: Boaz greets his reapers, "The LORD be with you," and they answer, "The LORD bless thee"—everyday greetings of faith.

Ruth 3.audience: The first Israelites who heard Ruth knew family members could redeem property and protect a household. They heard Ruth and Boaz seek that help with care and public responsibility.

culture.title: The threshing floor
culture.text: Grain was threshed and winnowed on a flat, open area, where the evening wind blew away the chaff. Owners slept there at harvest time to guard the grain.

culture.title: Spreading the skirt
culture.text: Ruth asks Boaz to spread his skirt (the corner of his garment) over her, an expression for taking a woman in marriage and under protection (compare Ezekiel 16:8).

Ruth 4.audience: The first Israelites who heard Ruth knew city gates were places for witnesses and legal decisions. They also knew David's family line and heard how Ruth became his great-grandmother.

culture.title: Business at the gate
culture.text: Legal matters were settled at the city gate before ten elders as witnesses.

culture.title: The sandal
culture.text: The text explains an older custom: a man gave his sandal to confirm the transfer of a right of redemption. Writing for later readers, it adds "this was the manner in former time in Israel."
